opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that an evaluation is really a statement about what we care about. AI models can be incredibly helpful in generating tasks, drafting rubrics, even grading at scale, and we use them a lot for that. But deciding *what* is worth measuring, and whether a task actually reflects real-world value, still benefits enormously from human judgment.

When we built evaluations grounded in real professional work, the most important input came from experts who actually do those jobs. A model can write something that *looks* like a realistic task for a lawyer or a nurse or an engineer, but an experienced practitioner will immediately notice when it's subtly off: the wrong kind of ambiguity, missing context that would matter in practice, or a "correct" answer that no one in the field would accept. Those details are exactly what separate a meaningful eval from one that just measures pattern-matching.

There's also a circularity problem. If models create the questions and models grade the answers, you risk baking in the same blind spots on both sides. The eval ends up rewarding whatever the models already find natural, and you lose the signal you were trying to get. Humans act as an outside anchor. They catch errors in the grading, notice when a model is gaming a rubric, and tell you when a high score doesn't translate into something people actually find useful.

So I see it as a partnership. Models give us scale and speed, and humans give us grounding and taste. As models get more capable, the oversight role shifts. It becomes less about writing every question by hand and more about verifying, auditing, and making sure we're still measuring the things that matter. But I don't think it goes away. If anything, the stakes of getting evaluation right only go up as these systems become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response explains why human judgment helps ground and audit evaluations, but does not say evaluation datasets may have fewer examples than training datasets or connect that to extensive human review.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that models are really good at generating things that look like evaluations, and that's actually the problem. When we ask a model to write a hundred tasks for, say, a coding benchmark, it will give us a hundred plausible tasks. But plausible isn't the bar. The bar is whether the task actually measures the thing we care about, whether the answer key is correct, and whether there's some shortcut that lets a model get the right answer for the wrong reason.

So where humans come in, in my experience, is in a few places. One is just ground truth. If you're building an eval for, say, expert-level questions in medicine or law, you want someone who actually knows that domain to look at the question and the reference answer and say, yes, that's right, and no, there isn't a second defensible answer we're going to unfairly penalize. Models can hallucinate a confident-sounding answer key, and if that's wrong, your whole eval is measuring agreement with an error.

The second is contamination and triviality. A model generating tasks tends to produce things close to its own training distribution, which means those tasks may be easy for it or for its successors in a way that doesn't reflect real capability. A human looking at it can say, this is basically a rephrasing of a well-known problem, or this is solvable by pattern matching on the wording.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is taste about what matters. The eval is supposed to be a proxy for something in the world. We care about whether a model can actually do useful work for a real person. A human reviewer has a much better sense of whether a task is representative of what people actually need, versus something that's technically hard but kind of artificial.

I'll also say it's not all-or-nothing. We use models heavily in the pipeline. They're great for first drafts, for scaling, for catching formatting issues, even for flagging questions that seem ambiguous. But the places where we've been burned, where an eval turned out to be noisy or saturated faster than it should have, almost always trace back to a step where nobody with real expertise looked carefully. So I think of human oversight less as a bottleneck and more as the thing that makes the number mean anything.

r001.rationale: The response explains human review as a way to verify accuracy, detect shortcuts, and assess real-world relevance, but it does not say evaluation datasets may have fewer examples than training datasets.

astra-6.text:
I think human oversight is valuable because models can help us generate evaluations, but they don’t necessarily know whether we’re asking the right questions. An evaluation might look reasonable and be easy to score, but still miss the behavior we actually care about.

Humans bring context about what matters in practice: what a good outcome looks like, which failures would be consequential, and where a test is ambiguous. So I see models as a way to scale the work—generating candidate questions or surfacing potential gaps—while humans help validate that we’re measuring something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says humans help validate meaningful evaluation questions, but it does not explain that evaluation datasets may receive extensive human review because they contain fewer examples than training datasets.

sol-6.1.text:
Human oversight is valuable because a model can help you generate a lot of evaluations, but you still need someone to ask: Are we testing the right thing? Does this reflect what users actually care about? And is the answer we’re treating as correct actually correct?

If a model creates an evaluation and then judges the results, it can carry the same blind spots through both steps. Humans can challenge those assumptions, catch ambiguous questions, and bring context that’s missing from the test. So I think of AI as helping us scale evaluation, while people help make sure the signal we’re getting is meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response supports human oversight by citing blind spots, ambiguity, and missing context, but it does not say evaluation datasets have fewer examples than training datasets or that they can receive extensive human review.
